text: I believe the cars can be measured, as a group not individually. Here is my idea: You take the roof of the walmart's color and the color of the pavement on a holiday (no cars in the lot). this should give you the average color of both. Then in future days when there are cars in the parking lot you can take the average color of the parking lot and this should give you a baseline for what a "normal" number of visitors look like. Every day the colors of the environment will change slightly (weather, clouds, seasons, etc) so you must find the deviation between the current roof color and the baseline roof color (taken earlier on a holiday) and do this each day so you can apply that shift to the parking lot sample as well. Then you compare the current colors to previous average colors and you can create a graph of the traffic over time. you will never know exactly how much traffic there is but it doesnt matter, all that matters is the change in traffic because that can tell you the change in the revenue. This approach is all relative but that's all you really need. The problem is that there is probably a significant margin of error, but a cool thought experiment nonetheless. P.S. I also forgot to mention that there is a reasonable doubt for this because for example what if a car is gray like the pavement? then it will be a false negative for traffic or what if there is 1 red car, 1 blue car, 1 green? This could be a huge issue but I think it is mitigated by the metallic/reflective nature of car paints, so even if the colors of the cars cancel out, the parking lot should see a bias towards white if more cars are there.

author: @user-6f8975
text: According to the efficient market hypothesis, prices react instantaneously to news. Although the EMH may not be 100% true, it's easy to verify that the price of many financial assets indeed react instantaneously to published financial news (i.e. the price moves just for 30-60 seconds or so). Have you tried trading the oil price (i.e. opening and then closing the position) in the 30-60 seconds right when the news is published? That would get rid of 99% of volatility of your first proposed strategy (which I reckon is trading oil and keeping the position open for one entire week), which could also explain why the strategy is not profitable due to volatility drag. EDIT: In other words, let's say the weekly change in oil stock determines 5% of the weekly movement in oil price, and all the other news and events determine the remaining 95%. If you trade for one entire week, your signal is submerged by the remaining causes of the movement of the oil price. Whereas, if you just trade in those 60 seconds, you are effectively isolating the signal and minimizing the volatility.
